title: Log Scales
objective: After this level you can read a chart where each step up the axis multiplies instead of adds, and explain when that helps.
summary: On a log scale each step multiplies, so 1 to 10 is as far as 10 to 100, and steady doubling becomes a straight line, as on Moore's 1965 chart.

cards.headline: In 1965, Gordon Moore drew explosive growth as a straight line.
cards.body: He was tracking transistors, the tiny switches on computer chips. The trick was in his axis: each step up it multiplied instead of adding.

cards.headline: Each step multiplies
cards.body: On an ordinary axis, each step up adds the same amount. On a log scale, each step multiplies: 1, 10, 100, 1,000. The gap from 1 to 10 is as wide as the gap from 100,000 to 1,000,000. That lets one chart fit a thousand, a million and a billion at equal steps, since each is 1,000 times the one before.

cards.headline: Straight means steady growth
cards.body: Here's the payoff. On an ordinary chart, something that doubles at a steady pace curves upward ever more steeply. On a log scale, that same growth becomes a straight line. That's what Moore's chart showed: the transistor count has doubled roughly every two years, and on a log axis the points line up.

cards.fact: Log scales are useful, and easy to misread.
cards.context: In a 2020 experiment, about 2,000 Americans saw COVID-19 deaths on either a log chart or an ordinary one. Asked a basic question about it, about 84% of the ordinary-chart group got it right, against about 41% of the log group. So check the axis labels first: if each step multiplies, read it that way.

cards.headline: Log scales: read
learned: 1 to 10 spans as far as 10 to 100
Check the labels before the slope

pairs.right: Each step up adds the same amount

questions.prompt: How does something that doubles at a steady pace look on a log-scale chart?

options.label: A curve that grows ever steeper
options.rationale: That's how it looks on an ordinary chart.

options.label: A line that rises then falls
A flat line
options.rationale: A flat line on a log scale means no growth.

questions.explanation: Steady doubling multiplies by the same amount each period, and a log axis turns equal multiplications into equal steps: a straight line.

questions.prompt: Where would a thousand, a million and a billion sit on a log axis?

options.label: At equal steps, since each is 1,000 times the last
Bunched together near the bottom
options.rationale: That's an ordinary axis, where a thousand and a million look tiny.

options.label: The billion would sit far off the top of the chart
options.rationale: A log axis fits all three easily.

questions.explanation: Each rung multiplies by 1,000, and a log axis spaces equal multiplications equally.
